questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
KUL is highly renowned academically, and I wanted to challenge myself and to try to study in a way that I wasn't accustomed to. 

Furthermore, I wanted to challenge myself by going to a place I'd never been before, where I had no network whatsover, and where I was forced to speak a lot of English if I had to establish one.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I was overall very pleased with the academic level of the institution, though some exams were tougher than others. I've also never had as stressful of an examination period before.

In the end, the best part of the experience was getting to know a ton of people from a lot of different places, many of whom have become close friends of mine.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
Very easy. Leuven is a massive student city with plenty of internationals, and both the university and the city authorities are used to having a lot of foreigners arriving every semester. The KUL-website is quite easy to navigate and often updated, and you're sent loads of e-mails and papers that aim to help you get settled quickly.

Both the university and the town authorities are also quick to answer any questions you may have.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Nothing in particular.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: See above. The university makes sure to keep in touch with you at a quite steady pace, and in the introduction week, there are several lectures intended to get you properly settled - both regarding your faculty, and your practicalities.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Very difficult. Unless you are adamant on having a room with your own bathroom, kitchen or similar, I strongly advise to get a room through one of the colleges that KUL offers. Whilst you're not guaranteed a room this way, the effort required is exponentially smaller than getting a proper studio on the private market.

The housing market in Leuven is dreadful, and you have to constantly survey different webpages and FaceBook-groups and make offers very quickly, whilst being wary of the many scammers on there. Finding accommodation is even more difficult at a distance, since you can't just schedule a showing. I ended up being very satisfied with my studio, having both my own bathroom, kitchenette and a larger bed, but it took a lot of time and effort to get there.

Overall, if you're not absolutely wanting certain amenities in your room, I would advise trying to secure housing via the colleges available through KUL.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Prices are higher and it's more difficult to secure something proper, but you might get something that's a lot more spacious and with more facilities than the rooms offered by KUL.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As mentioned, the housing market is awful. The rooms available by KUL seem generally to be fairly decent, though bathrooms (including toilets) and kitchens are shared. Prices are quite affordable, being at around 500-550 € on average, I believe.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
As with getting settled, both the university and the city authorities are accustomed to having many people register and often.

For university, you have to set up your university and grab your university card.

For the city authorities, you have to make an appointment at the town hall, have a chat with a clerk, and file some papers.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I don't remember too much of it, but for university, you have to create your university user and file some practical information, and subsequently grab your student card.

For the town hall, see above. After the process, a police officer would come by your home at an undisclosed time to ensure you're actually staying there.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Plenty of brochures, webpages etc. Furthermore, both the university and city authorities were quick to answer any questions you may have.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
Almost wholly succesfull. As far as I know, there's no limit on how many students can attend a given class - classes are mostly lectures, in which the professor talks in an auditorium with limited individual participation from students. 

The difficulty stems firstly from getting a combination of courses to reach a total of 30 ECTS-points, while simultaneously not having the courses overlap. Many of the English-language courses are held on the same days, so there likely will be some overlap. Planning your courses will likely take a few hours.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Pick up your student card as quickly as possible, as you'll use it to enter certain facilities like university libraries, as well as to attend certain events.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Professors are overall very knowledgeable and courses are interesting. Some courses have a lot more difficult exams than others.

The amount of points awarded for a course often do not correspond to the effort required to be put in - a 6-point ECTS course is NOT twice as difficult  or time-consuming as a 3-point ECTS course.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The academic level is like in Denmark, but the main spike in difficulty consists of the number of courses required to be enrolled in. Courses award ECTS points at 3, 4 or 6 points, so you'll have to attend quite a few courses. 

Not all courses require preparation prior to classes, but it goes without saying that a collective curriculum of 6+ courses makes for a lot of required material to study in the examination periods.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The teaching is based on lectures, in which the professor talks aloud to students in an auditorium. Questions are welcome and usually encouraged, but generally no individiual participation is required.

The curriculum is usually the slides that the professor brings as well as what the professor says during class. There's often no textbook.

I rather missed the teaching method at UCPH, in which most classes are seminars with more interactivity and a more informal setting.

When it comes to grades, it seems to me that for quite a few classes, the difficulty subsists first in passing, and then getting a good grade - this is not the case for all classes, but for some, you genuinely worry that you won't pass your exams, despite putting in a lot of time and effort.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Private International Law

Judicial Protection in the European Union

European Company Law

European Contract Law

EU Economic Law

Restorative Justice

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Private International Law is very interesting, but the level of abstraction is very high in many parts of the course and the grades granted are notoriously low. Professor Van Calster told is in the first lecture that the rate of passing the course was about 65%, with pre-Covid levels being around 75%. The course focuses on jurisdiction and applicable law in international disputes with focus on the Brussels Ia-Regulation, Rome I and Rome II Regulation as well as case law of the CJEU, so while the subject is very good to be familiar with, the low average grade and possibility to fail makes it difficult for me to recommend it. If you do so, be aware that the exam requires a lot of preparation. Note that professor Van Calster is going on a one-year sabbatical as of Summer 2024, so your experience may be different.

European Contract Law is very intense as it is placed over the course of two weeks entirely, despite being a 6-point ECTS course. You will have to take into account that some classes will have to be skipped, and depending on if courses are recorded, you will have to prioritise. Professor Kadner Graziano is very knowledgeable, incredibly friendly and encourages student participation and discussion, and the course itself gives very useful and fascinating insight into the contract law of not just European, but international jurisdictions. The exam requires a good amount of preparation, but if prepared correctly, is quite managable. I highly recommend the course.

Judicial Protection in the European Union revolved around what actions can be brought to the CJEU, and how its inner workings are. The course included a voluntary excursion to the CJEU (with limited possible spaces - be quick to reserve when they're offered!), and was quite interesting. Do note that professor Wathelet had his last semester of teaching as of Spring of 2024, and I believe the course will change quite a bit from now. It's difficult to say how and what will change, so whereas I'd normally recommend it, I don't know what the course will look like in the Autumn semester of 2024.

European Company Law was interesting, and mostly focused on the European directives attempting to harmonise company law throughout the EU. If you're already familiar with company law (which I recommend being, and which the course itself states as a prerequisite), this will be a good way to get insight on the background legislation of the articles in your national company law. The examination is oral, and while rather tough, you do get to use all PowerPoints and other notes in your preparation time.

EU Economic Law is similar to European Company Law, but focuses on competition law, and secondly on the internal market and the free movement of goods, services and establishment. While I'd usually recommend the course, professor Devroe had his last semester of teaching as of Spring 2024, so I don't know what changes will be made to course.

Restorative Justice is interesting enough, but I wasn't that big of a fan. It's a criminology course so the method was unfamiliar to me. The exam being given via a mix of class participation, a 10-page paper and a presentation is a good way to mix up the mostly handwritten, 3-hour exams, however. Recommended if you need to get rid of 6 ECTS-points and feel like trying something that isn't law.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Lunch and having an evening beer became very frequent social activities, and while neither were particularly costly in themselves, their frequency added quite a bit to costs.

My rent was about 40-50% higher than what would've been paid if I got a room through KUL, but in exchange I got my own bathroom, kitchenette, a bigger bed etc., and therefore the costs were expected.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Groceries are generally the same price as in Denmark. Meat might occassionally be more expensive. 

Beer is a lot cheaper, particularly when compared to the styles being offered. Whilst a regular lager might not be that much cheaper, some of the heavy trappist beers are both more widely available and significantly cheaper.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
KUL offers a sports club for cheap, granting you access to loads of different facilities and sports. The sporting facility is very nice, with loads of different possibilities.

Student organisations like the Erasmus Student Network and Pangaea constantly host different social events of all sorts, making it very easy to attend events with other internationals. Furthermore, Pangaea is placed in the middle of the city, and is a good hang-out spot for internationals.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All sorts. The sports card provides access to the entirety of the sporting facility, and the different student organisations host a wide variety of different events - excursions, sporting events, pub-crawls, social gatherings, language-learning events etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Attend as many events during the introduction week as you can. You will likely meet a lot of your very good friends there, and since the Belgian and the international students mostly keep to their own groups, it's granted that you'll see some of the people you meet again and again during your exchange.

Take advantage of the different events on offer throughout the semester as well, and do attend a cantus. If possible, try to go to a more private one.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Belgium is very nicely connected by train, and via the national railway services, NSCB, you can get some very cheap tickets (6,50-7,50 €) going anywhere in the country. Brussels is just over 20 minutes away, but Ghent, Antwerp, Brügge, Dinant, Namur and similar are all very nice day trips.

Other than that, enjoy the events on offer and time with your friends. Belgian students go home on the weekends, so the city is mostly locals and international students on Friday evenings through Sunday afternoons.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Rather easy. Belgium doesn't differ that much from Denmark, and even then, I rarely socialised with Belgians. It was a predominantly international environment, with no one culture needing to be adjusted to.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: No. Belgian students are a lot more prone to be open and speaking English while inebriated, so you might have a chat at a fakbar or similar. Otherwise, not really.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None in particular.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The beer culture for sure. Very easily available, affordable, and varied. I highly recommend stepping a bit out of your comfort zone and trying some things you haven't before - the variety is incredible.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
If you decide to go to KUL, be prepared for an academically challenging exchange. You're not guaranteed to pass your exams, and you will have to put in a lot of effort to pass all 30 ECTS points. That being said, it's in no way impossible, and the amount of international friends you'll make who will be suffering through the same with you makes it and your relationship with them all the more special.

Be proactive, both socially and academically. Everyone's on equal footing, and people are incredibly nice and helpful.

Be sure to relax and enjoy your time there. An Erasmus is a fantastic opportunity to get to know a lot of great people, so while the studying might be challenging, always remember to take good breaks and unwind.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be certain that you want to also have a rather hectic exchange when choosing KUL. Read other travel reports and experience reports.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: While I aimed to go to KUL for the academic challenge, I found that the biggest benefit from having gone there was the many friends and experiences I made during my stay. It was incredibly rewarding to get a close relationship with people from many different places, particularly other citizens of the European Union, with which you share rights, political systems, legislation etc.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: While it's incredibly daunting to go to a foreign country with an unfamiliar way of studying, entirely without a network, it all becomes surprisingly easy very quickly. Adjusting to everything is difficult at first, but before long, everything becomes familiar. There are lots of people around to support you as well.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
